articles.title: A Florida family kept a 498-acre cattle operation for generations as development spread around it; the ranch is now permanently protected through a $7.48 million conservation easement
articles.summary: A 498-acre cattle ranch in Florida's Martin County, known as Turnpike Dairy, secures its future through a $7.48 million conservation easement, ensuring the continuation of agriculture amidst urban development.
articles.body: A 498-acre cattle ranch in Florida’s Martin County has been permanently protected from future development through a $7.48 million conservation easement, allowing the family that has managed the property for generations to continue its agricultural operations.Known as Turnpike Dairy, the ranch will remain in private ownership under the agreement, with Martin County contributing $3.74 million towards the easement. The property includes grazing pasture, wetlands and bayheads that provide wildlife habitat.The ranch is among several agricultural properties approved for protection under Florida’s Rural and Family Lands Protection Program, which seeks to preserve working farms and ranches as development pressure increases.Conservation deal keeps ranch in agricultural useTurnpike Dairy lies within the Florida Wildlife Corridor and borders conservation land managed by the South Florida Water Management District. It is also close to other properties covered by conservation easements, helping maintain connections between protected areas.The property contains improved pasture alongside scattered wetlands and bayheads, which support wildlife and contribute to the wider landscape.The ranch is enrolled in the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services’ Best Management Practices programme, which promotes agricultural practices designed to protect natural resources.Under a rural lands protection easement, development rights are purchased to prevent future development while allowing farming and ranching to continue. The land remains privately owned rather than being transferred to the state.Florida programme has protected more than 251,000 acresFlorida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson announced on September 29. that the governor and Cabinet had approved the preservation of more than 4,500 acres of agricultural land through the Rural and Family Lands Protection Program.Established in 2001 under the Rural and Family Lands Protection Act, the programme works with farmers and ranchers to keep agricultural properties in production while protecting natural resources.Simpson said the arrangement allows Florida to conserve working land without removing it from private ownership or creating the long-term maintenance costs associated with state-owned conservation properties.Since the programme began, more than 251,000 acres of working agricultural land have been permanently preserved, including nearly 186,000 acres during Simpson’s tenure, according to the department.Other properties approved for protection include Blandford Farm & Ranch, a 349-acre sod and hay farm in Lake County, and Encore Farms, a 194-acre horse and cattle operation in the same county. Fair Bluff Ranch, a 618-acre cattle property in Martin County, was also included in the approvals.The agreements are intended to keep agricultural operations viable while limiting the conversion of working land to other uses.You use AI every day. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke shot back at the Delhi Police after they released a video claiming that while under detention, he was offered to speak to his family after his grandmother's demise.Dipke disputed the force's claim that he had declined assistance to contact his relatives and travel home for her last rites, saying he wasn't given his phone to access contacts.In a statement reacting to the police's account, Dipke said he had repeatedly requested access to his phone to retrieve his cousin's number and speak to a lawyer, but was denied both requests. He also questioned why officers asked him to call his father at 3.30 am and tell him that he could be sent to jail for a long time."I had requested to let me speak to my cousin who lives with my grandmother. Asked for my phone just for a couple of minutes so I could at least take out the number of my cousin.""Why Delhi Police didn’t let me use my phone? I had also asked for a call with lawyer which was again denied."Dipke said the call to his father was particularly distressing because his family had just lost his grandmother."At 3.30 in the morning, Delhi Police asks me to call my father and inform him that tomorrow I’ll be going in jail for a long time. The same father who has just lost his mother. How much more trauma did you want to put my family through after we already lost my grandmother?"Questioning the timing and purpose of the call, he added, "What was the purpose of trying to call my parents at f-ing 3:30 in the morning? You wanted to torment them?"Police say Dipke declined assistanceDipke's allegations came after Delhi Police released a video showing officers informing him of his grandmother's death while he was in detention in the national capital.Deputy Commissioner of Police Neha Yadav said officers approached the CJP founder after learning about the death and offered to help him contact his family, arrange flights and travel to his hometown for the funeral. According to the police, he declined the assistance.“As soon as the Delhi Police received information about the passing away of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) Founder Abhijeet Dipke's grandmother, officers approached him to convey this sad news and offered all possible assistance. They sensitively asked if he needed help with flights, phone calls, or anything else. They repeatedly asked if he wished to speak to his parents, but he declined,” DCP Yadav said.The police released the video after Dipke's mother, Anita Dipke, accused the force of lying about informing her son of the death. She had said the family was unable to contact him and had postponed the last rites until he could return home.Delhi Police maintained that Dipke had been informed about his grandmother's death and the scheduled funeral. articles.title: In 1946, a collector bought a Ming-era cloisonné pomegranate box for £19; 77 years later, it was found in an attic, auctioneers expected £6,000 to £10,000 before bidding pushed it to £288,000
articles.summary: A cloisonné pomegranate box from the Ming dynasty, bought for £19 in 1946, sells for a staggering £288,000 after being found in an attic, showcasing its incredible value and historical significance.
articles.body: A Chinese enamel box bought for £19 at a London auction in 1946 has sold for £288,000 after being rediscovered in a family attic, where it had remained largely unnoticed for decades.The 15th-century object, known as a cloisonné pomegranate box, went under the hammer at Dreweatts auction house in Berkshire with an estimate of £6,000 to £10,000. Competitive bidding pushed the final price far beyond that range, with an Asian private collector securing the piece.The box belonged to Major Edward Copleston Radcliffe, who bought it at Sotheby’s in 1946. After he died in 1967, it remained among other objects in his collection until his family sent the items to Dreweatts for assessment.Rare Chinese box dates back to 15th centuryDreweatts specialists Mark Newstead and Yingwen Tao recognised the box’s significance during their examination of the collection. The piece dates to the Ming dynasty and bears the reign mark of Xuande, the fifth emperor of the dynasty, who ruled from 1426 to 1435.The box was made in the 15th century in imperial workshops near Beijing’s Forbidden City, according to the auction house. It is decorated with pomegranates, branches and blossoms. The fruit was associated with fertility in Chinese symbolism.Cloisonné is a decorative technique in which thin metal strips form compartments that are filled with enamel. Early Ming examples bearing the Xuande mark are particularly scarce, as production was closely controlled by the imperial court.Newstead, Dreweatts’ director of Asian ceramics and works of art, said the box’s discovery among less valuable items in an attic was remarkable.He said the auction attracted strong competition from nine telephone bidders before a private collector in Asia won the lot.One of few surviving examplesThe box is among a small number of known examples of Xuande-marked pomegranate boxes. According to Dreweatts, only five are known to exist, with three held by museums or other institutions and one in another private collection.The newly rediscovered box had previously been displayed at the National Gallery of South Africa during a Chinese exhibition in Cape Town in 1953. It was subsequently believed to have been lost from public view.Its sale price of £288,000 was substantially above the upper estimate of £10,000. The result also returned the object to the auction market for the first time since Radcliffe purchased it in 1946.“There was very strong bidding between nine telephone bidders, with a private collector in Asia finally winning out,” Newstead said.You use AI every day. articles.title: One Indian killed, 10 injured in Riyadh airport strike; chilling video shows aftermath
articles.summary: An Indian national was killed and 10 others injured in a missile strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport that killed 13 people and wounded
articles.body: An Indian national was killed and 10 others injured in a missile strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300 others, India's embassy in Saudi Arabia said, a day after the deadly attack.The Embassy of India in Riyadh said it had been following up on Saturday's attack and was in touch with local authorities and hospital officials to enquire about the condition of the injured Indians.“Our officials have also reached out to the hospital authorities. We will provide further updates as they become available,” the embassy said in a statement.In a later update the embassy confirmed that one Indian national succumbed to injuries."It is learnt that one Indian national injured in the Riyadh attack has unfortunately lost his life today. We convey our heartfelt condolences to the family of the deceased. We are in touch with the family and will provide all support for ensuring the early repatriation of mortal remains," the embassy said.In a post on X, external affairs minister S Jaishankar condoled the death writing, "Deeply grieved at the loss of life of an Indian national in the Riyadh attack. My heartfelt condolences to the bereaved family. The Embassy will extend all possible assistance."An eyewitness video released by Reuters captured the chilling aftermath of the strike, showing large boards and debris scattered across the terminal floor as people moved through a dust-filled hall.The Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said on Sunday that an unidentified projectile had struck a passenger terminal at the airport. The latest incident came less than 24 hours after Saturday's missile strike killed 13 people, making it the deadliest attack in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began.There were no immediate details about Sunday's strike, which hit the same complex housing terminals 3 and 4, used for domestic flights. The airport remained closed as authorities moved schools in Riyadh to online classes.The Saudi statement on Saturday's fatalities identified the dead as four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals and one each from Palestine, the US, Egypt, Jordan, Syria and Sudan. The victims included Egyptian flight attendant Azza Ramzy, who worked for Saudi airline Flynas, and Syrian national Buthaina Ahmad Oweida, a widowed mother of four.The Houthis have acknowledged targeting Saudi airports and oil installations in recent days, although they have not claimed responsibility for Saturday's deadly airport strike. On Sunday, the group's military spokesperson, Brigadier General Yahya Saree, warned airlines and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, saying they were vulnerable to attacks. Airports in Mecca and Medina were exempt from the warning.The escalation has raised concerns over regional aviation, global oil supplies and shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key route connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis and planned to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.You use AI every day. articles.body: Realtor.com reported that Mike “The Miz” Mizanin bought his Laurel Canyon home in the Hollywood Hills for $1,865,000 in 2012. Forbes reported that the renovated and expanded property was listed for $3.65 million in 2017, while Variety reported in 2019 that it sold for just over $3 million.The listing highlighted a basketball court, pool and spaForbes described the Hollywood Hills West property as Mediterranean-style, with four bedrooms and three and a half bathrooms. The listing, handled by Victoria Mirisch of Pinnacle Estate Properties, highlighted a basketball court, swimming pool and spa. Wrestling Online reported that the house measured 4,532 square feet and included three levels, a circular driveway, a home theater and mountain views.In Property Renovations and Their Impact on House Price Index Construction, Federal Housing Finance Agency economists Alexander N. Bogin and William M. Doerner found that failing to account for property improvements can overstate repeat-sales house price index estimates, with valuation distortions reaching 15 percent in central districts of large cities. These numbers are not national averages, and the authors admit they were unable to segregate the renovations by quality, degree, or expense.In Property Renovations and Their Impact on House Price Index Construction, Federal Housing Finance Agency economists Alexander N. Bogin and William M. Doerner found that failing to account for property improvements can overstate repeat-sales house price index estimates, with valuation distortions reaching 15 percent in central districts of large cities. These numbers are not national averages, and the authors admit they were unable to segregate the renovations by quality, degree, or expense.Overlooked renovations can overstate price growth by as much as 15 percent in central districts of large citiesThe Federal Housing Finance Agency’s working paper Property Renovations and Their Impact on House Price Index Construction, by economists Alexander N. Bogin and William M. Doerner, looked at how renovations affect repeat-sales house price indices. The paper says renovation activity can create positive quality drift in repeat-sales indices, and that omitting those improvements can push local price estimates upward by as much as 15 percent in central districts of large cities. It also finds the distortion fades outside downtown areas and is generally negligible in smaller cities with populations below 500,000. These are index-construction results and do not measure the value of Mizanin’s house. The $3.65 million asking price followed a renovation and expansion, so the paper offers background on how improvements can distort price data, not an estimate for this property.A study of 780 English sales found homes sold at about 96 percent of the listing priceIn Bargaining over Residential Real Estate: Evidence from England, Antonio Merlo and François Ortalo-Magné examined how asking prices play out. The data covered 780 properties listed and sold through four real estate agencies from June 1995 through April 1998. The properties sold at an average of around 96 percent of their listing price within 11 weeks of listing. They found that a higher listing price led to fewer viewings, higher offers, a higher sale price and a longer time on the market. The longer a property stayed listed, the lower its sale price relative to the asking price. The sample is a restricted comparison: the average starting listing price was £69,812, and the market was England in the 1990s, not Los Angeles.Variety reported that the house sold for just over $3 millionVariety reported in 2019 that Mizanin and his wife, Maryse Mizanin, owned the Laurel Canyon property from 2012 until its sale, and that the “quasi-Tuscan mini-estate” sold for just over $3 million to a non-famous married couple. Forbes had called the house Mediterranean-style, so the style label varies by source. The sale price was a little over four-fifths of the $3.65 million asking price.You use AI every day. articles.title: Ukraine steps up attacks on Russian tech infrastructure, damages third data center
articles.summary: A Ukrainian drone strike damaged a data center operated by Russian technology major Yandex, forcing it to suspend operations, the company said on Sunday.
articles.body: A Ukrainian drone strike damaged a data center operated by Russian technology major Yandex, forcing it to suspend operations, the company said on Sunday. The incident marked the third attack on the company's facilities in four days as Kyiv expands its strikes on infrastructure located deep inside Russian territory.The strike on the facility in Vladimir, east of Moscow, disrupted several Yandex services. Russian independent news outlet Astra reported that users across dozens of Russian cities, as well as in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia, were unable to book taxis or access banking services.Russia and Ukraine continue to engage in long-range aerial attacks even as fighting along much of the frontline remains largely deadlocked, more than four and a half years after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion. Kyiv's latest strikes on data centers follow Russian attacks on similar infrastructure in Ukraine.“ As a result of the drone attack, the infrastructure of Yandex's data center in Vladimir was damaged. Operations at the data center have been completely halted. There were no injuries,” Yandex Cloud said in a post on Telegram, where it provides updates on service disruptions.The latest incident follows two attacks on Yandex facilities earlier in the week. A drone strike on Thursday forced the company to take a data centre in the Ryazan region, south-east of Moscow, offline. On Friday, Ukrainian drones targeted its major facility in the Kaluga region, south-west of the capital, partially disrupting operations, the company said.Often compared with Google, Yandex operates Russia's leading search engine alongside a broad portfolio of digital services. The company is also a major participant in the country's artificial intelligence sector.The attack occurred a day after US President Donald Trump called for Ukraine to elect a new leader, criticising President Volodymyr Zelenskyy over his handling of efforts to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the United States, according to AP.“I suggest they get a new leader, who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does,” Trump said on Saturday.Trump's remarks came after he reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday to purchase diesel from Russia in a bid to ease rising fuel costs ahead of the US midterm elections. For several weeks, Trump has pressed Zelenskyy to halt attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.The US president has attributed record-high diesel prices in the United States to Ukrainian strikes rather than the US-led war in Iran, which has pushed up global energy costs. Ukrainian and European officials have expressed concern over the diesel agreement, arguing that the arrangement could provide financial support for Russia's war effort.Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha rejected Trump's criticism in a post on X late Saturday, saying Zelenskyy was leading the country in its fight for independence and continued to enjoy public backing.“He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well,” Sybiha wrote.Meanwhile, search and rescue operations concluded in the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia following a Russian bombing on Saturday, Ivan Fedorov, the former regional head and co-chair of the regional defence council, said on Sunday.The attack killed 20 people, including four children, while more than 30 others were injured, Fedorov said. Eight of the wounded remained in hospital.Separately, a Ukrainian drone strike in Russia's border region of Bryansk killed a man and injured two women, local officials said on Sunday.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1993, Bill Clinton proposed a Pacific Northwest forest plan after a bitter logging fight; the final 1994 framework covered about 24.5 million federal acres
articles.summary: In 1993, President Bill Clinton initiated a groundbreaking forest management strategy in the Pacific Northwest amid conflicts between timber industry and environmentalists, ultimately adopting the Northwest Forest Plan in 1994, protecting 24.5 million acres of federal forestland.
articles.body: In 1993, US President Bill Clinton encountered a bitter conflict in the Pacific Northwest, where timber workers and logging companies clashed with environmentalists over the future of the region’s old-growth forests. Timber sales were disrupted because of the dispute. Additionally, it affected forest-dependent communities and eventually triggered legal battles over the protection of threatened wildlife.On July 1, 1993, Clinton announced a proposed forest-management strategy which intended to balance timber production, environmental safeguards and economic support for the affected communities. In 1994, the final Northwest Forest Plan was adopted. This established a management framework for approximately 24.5 million acres of federal forestland in western Washington, western Oregon and northwestern California.Why the Pacific Northwest turned into a battlegroundThe differences had developed over years of intensive timber harvesting and disagreements about how federal forests should be managed. Logging provided employment and supported local businesses; however, environmentalists and scientists cautioned that the loss of old-growth forests threatened wildlife habitats, waterways and broader forest ecosystems. The northern spotted owl became a central focus of the dispute as it depended heavily on mature forest habitat and was listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act.The Clinton administration’s July 1993 background briefing described a region-wide dispute that involved the protection of old-growth forests, fish, wildlife and water, alongside workers’ economic needs, businesses and communities dependent on timber. The administration also identified the marbled murrelet and certain fish species as requiring protection.The then-president sought a response that would address both environmental concerns and economic uncertainty. In April 1993, Clinton brought representatives of different interest groups together at a Forest Conference in Portland, Oregon. After the conference, the administration assembled the Forest Ecosystem Management Assessment Team, a group of scientists and resource professionals tasked with evaluating management options for federal forests.The plan proposed protection across 24.5 million acresThe preferred approach announced by the administration was based on the team's watershed-oriented Option Nine. This proposal intended to create a better coordinated system for managing federal forests, with decisions informed by ecological conditions and the needs of individual watersheds. It aimed to establish a predictable, sustainable level of timber production while protecting important old-growth habitat and reducing conflicts between federal agencies over forest policy. This announcement was a proposal, not the date on which the final Northwest Forest Plan was adopted.The plan covered approximately 24.5 million acres of forest land under the federal government within the range of the northern spotted owl in the Pacific Northwest. However, different rules applied to different regions. These included late-successional reserves designed to conserve older forest habitat, riparian reserves intended to protect streams and surrounding areas, adaptive management areas for testing management approaches, and a matrix of lands where timber production could continue under the proposal’s guidelines. Therefore, the area was not put under one uniform protection regime; instead, management depended on the designation and its objectives.Though the northern spotted owl helped bring the conflict into the public eye, the proposed guidelines went further, considering the health of regional ecosystems more broadly. The framework for the proposal included protection for old-growth forest ecosystems, streams, watersheds, salmon, and other organisms. The overall philosophy behind the proposal was to manage the forests as systems.Following the development of the proposed approach, the administration prepared environmental impact statements and continued to work on implementation. On April 13, 1994, the secretaries of Agriculture and the Interior signed the Record of Decision for the plan, thus formalising the framework for federal forest management.Economic assistance and continuing disputesThe administration provided economic support as an important part of the response. Some of the measures that were undertaken include retraining workers for new industries, helping local businesses expand and diversify, and funding community-development initiatives. The purpose of this was to assist timber-dependent people to adapt to reduced timber harvest by the federal government.The proposal also faced legal and political challenges after its adoption. On December 21, 1994, a federal district court ruling upheld the administration’s approach, allowing implementation to continue. While the decision was a crucial legal milestone, it did not imply that disagreements regarding logging, conservation or the economic consequences of forest policy had disappeared.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Our seas, our land’: Sri Lanka assures India against hostile acts from its territory
articles.summary: Sri Lankan President Anura Kumara Dissanayake has assured that his country will not allow its territory or airspace to be used for activities that
articles.body: Sri Lankan President Anura Kumara Dissanayake has assured that his country will not allow its territory or airspace to be used for activities that threaten India's security, reiterating Colombo's commitment to a strict non-aligned foreign policy amid the ongoing US-Iran conflict.Addressing a public gathering at Nikaweratiya in Sri Lanka's Northwestern Province on Sunday, Dissanayake said the country would not permit hostile actions against its neighbour.“Our seas, our land would never be allowed to be used for any hostile act against our neighbour India,” he said, according to news agency PTI.Recalling his government's foreign policy record over the past two years, Dissanayake said Sri Lanka would continue to follow a non-aligned approach and would not take sides in military conflicts.“We are not a nation of any military capabilities, so we would not become party to any military conflict,” he said.Sri Lanka rejects requests from US, IranDissanayake said Sri Lanka had rejected requests from both the United States and Iran amid the ongoing conflict between the two sides.He said Colombo had denied permission for US aircraft to land in Sri Lanka and also turned down Iran's request to send warships.“But we won’t hesitate when asked for humanitarian assistance,” the Sri Lankan president said.In March, Sri Lanka provided hospital care to sailors from an Iranian vessel that was struck by a US submarine.India, Sri Lanka reaffirm security cooperationDissanayake's latest remarks follow a meeting with Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh in Colombo last month, during which the two sides discussed their broad partnership, including cooperation on regional safety, security, peace and prosperity.During the meeting, Dissanayake reiterated that Sri Lanka would not allow its territory to be used for activities inimical to India's security interests.Singh, who was on a three-day visit to Sri Lanka, also conveyed Prime Minister Narendra Modi's greetings to Dissanayake and congratulated him on completing two years in office.The two countries reaffirmed their commitment to working together as close neighbours and maritime partners for the development and welfare of their people, while supporting regional security.Dissanayake's latest statement reiterates Colombo's position that its territory and airspace will not be used for hostile activities against India, while maintaining its stated policy of staying out of military conflicts.You use AI every day. articles.title: Saudi Arabia will have to respond to Houthi airport attack - but the choices are stark
articles.summary: As Saudi Arabia reckons with the deadliest attack on its soil in more than a decade, questions swirl over how Riyadh will respond as Yemen’s Iran-allied Hout...
articles.body:
As Saudi Arabia reckons with the deadliest attack on its soil in more than a decade, questions swirl over how Riyadh will respond as Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis continue to wreak havoc on the kingdom.

The kingdom launched a major offensive last week to support Yemeni government forces fighting the Houthis, but the rebels have so far held their ground.

Instead, they have escalated their campaign against the kingdom, culminating in Saturday's missile attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport that killed at least 12 people.

Drawing from Iran's playbook in its conflict with the United States, the Houthis are vowing a painful escalation, targeting critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and imposing a global economic cost.

The Houthis have longstanding grievances against Saudi Arabia over Riyadh's decade-long war against the group, which triggered the world's worst humanitarian crisis. The recent Houthi escalation, however, is increasingly seen as an extension of Iran's conflict with Washington.

After eleven years of trying to contain the Houthi advance militarily and through talks, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and his brother, Defense Minister Khaled bin Salman, face limited options. Across the border, the rebels have grown more powerful, consolidating control over major cities and pushing to seize others, such as the densely populated Taiz.

"This threat has to be dealt with once and for all," Ali Shihabi, an author and commentator on Saudi politics told CNN. "A lot will depend on the performance of the Yemeni government troops on the ground and Saudi is helping them extensively with air power."

So far , Saudi Arabia has largely confined its role to providing air cover for the anti-Houthi Yemeni coalition, stopping short of any major deployment of its own troops on the ground. Whether that restraint will hold after Saturday's strike on Riyadh remains an open question.

Sending large numbers of Saudi troops into Yemen would plunge the kingdom into a an expensive and grinding ground war across rugged terrain and undercut the image Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is carefully cultivating of a stable, investment-friendly kingdom and global tourism hub.

Barely two decades ago, the Houthis were little more than a small religious revivalist movement. With Iranian backing, they have since grown into a formidable fighting force in possession of ballistic missiles and capable of striking as far away as Tel Aviv.

"They've developed their warfare," a southern Yemeni official who fought the Houthis for years told CNN. "They've gotten more sophisticated in their attacks, they're persistent and they've enhanced their intelligence."

Yemen's government alleges that Houthi rebels have worked with Iranian Revolutionary Guard experts to modify missiles into more effective weapons.

The new missiles fly faster and use a thermal-tracking system to home in on any heat source, Majed al-Nazili, spokesperson for the Yemen's armed forces, said. It remains unclear whether such missiles were used during Saturday's attack on Riyadh airport.

The Houthis' pursuit of more sophisticated weapons may now be extending into artificial intelligence.

AI company Anthropic said a group based in northern Yemen used its Claude AI tools to help develop guidance software for rockets and missiles – the systems that steer and stabilize the weapons in flight. The report did not identify those involved, but their location in Houthi-controlled northern Yemen suggests a possible link to the rebels.

Saudi Arabia has sought support from partners across the world to counter the group. France, Britain and Pakistan have committed support, while other allies like Turkey are considering sending help.

Prince Mohammed has also reportedly turned to Syria for help. Its president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, had led armed factions that successfully drove Iranian-backed groups from Syria after nearly a decade of civil war.

Yet Riyadh's biggest ally, the US, has not supported air strikes on the Houthis, instead sending more than 100 military advisers to provide intelligence under a newly formed joint command.

Last year Washington reached a ceasefire with the Iran-backed group that reopened the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the maritime chokepoint through which global trade flows between Asia and Europe, to US vessels. Prince Mohammed spoke twice with Trump last month , urging him to strike the Houthis, sources told CNN at the time, but the president declined to intervene.

"Clearly, direct US involvement via air power would help because US aircraft can respond to US satellite intelligence more rapidly," Shihabi said. "Saudi aircraft… are one stop removed from that loop so US involvement would be helpful."

Saudi Arabia, one of the largest countries in the Middle East, remains vulnerable despite procuring some of the most advanced US air defenses. Its infrastructure, which carries rich resources across vast desert terrain, leaves it an easy target for the cheaper one-way drones developed by the Houthis.

Among those killed in the Houthi attack on the Riyadh airport was an American citizen, the Saudi civil aviation body said Sunday – an attack that might draw Trump further into the war.

"The Saudis are good fighters," Trump told reporters following the attack. "But I think the attack was a terrible thing."

Asked whether the US will join strikes on the Houthis, the US president said: "We may"

articles.title: In 2021, California tested asphalt mixed with torn-up roofing shingles on State Route 49; all four mixes met performance specifications, but field results varied
articles.summary: In a groundbreaking pilot project, California has successfully incorporated recycled roofing shingles into asphalt on State Route 49. The project, monitored by UC researchers, meets state performance standards and offers promising insights into sustainable road construction.
articles.body: Ten million tonnes of outdated asphalt shingles are thought to wind up in landfills in the US each year. That is a wasteful practice because asphalt, the sticky binder that holds a road surface together, makes up 20 to 30% of a typical shingle. Despite the fact that highway engineers had been aware of this for decades, the majority of agencies continued to exercise caution when installing crushed roof tear-offs on crowded public roadways. No one wants to learn that lesson on a state highway, where the wrong mix can lead to broken surfaces, early repairs and paying for the work twice.California finally tried it in November 2021. Crews paved four short test sections on State Route 49 in El Dorado County, in the Sierra Nevada foothills just south of Placerville. At the same time, researchers from the University of California Pavement Research Centre monitored the work for Caltrans. In their report, every mix submitted for approval and quality control, including those with ground-up shingles, passed the state’s two performance-related tests. That is a clear pass in the laboratory. Since then, the road itself has told a more complicated story.What went on the road Each of the four sections ran about 1,000 feet (roughly 300 metres) along a winding climb with sharp curves, and the old surface beneath them was far from perfect. Before paving, the road had fatigue cracking in the wheel paths, age-related transverse and block cracks, and asphalt that varied in thickness from place to place.Every part had a different recipe. One was a control mix containing no recycled material at all. A second used 10 per cent recycled asphalt pavement, the ordinary blend already used on the rest of the job. A third had 3 per cent shingles, and the fourth mixed 10 per cent recycled pavement with 3 per cent shingles, all assessed by the weight of the stone. Some 360 tons (approximately 330 tonnes) of each mix was placed on 2 and 3 November 2021, and the report states that there were no serious issues in production or paving.Because shingle asphalt is old and rigid, the contractor used a softer base binder in the recycled mixes and added a tall oil rejuvenating agent. It worked, perhaps a little too well. The binder in the shingle mixtures tested slightly stiffer than the contract called for at high temperatures, although the finished mixes still passed the state’s performance-related tests. That stiffness helps against rutting, but it is the kind of detail engineers watch when they think about cracking later on.Why shingles are a tricky componentThe core problem is that asphalt exposed on a roof for years becomes oxidised, stiff and brittle. Markets for recycled shingles are limited, according to a 2021 white paper from CalRecycle, the state’s recycling agency. The paper says shingles in asphalt mixtures have mostly been used as a source of aggregate, not as a replacement binder, because oxidation makes the asphalt binder difficult to reuse. It adds that the state has already been studying these constraints in practice, and it frames recycled shingles as a limited feedstock rather than a direct binder substitute. It also points to the scale of the waste stream, with an estimated 687,155 tonnes of roofing shingles landfilled in California in 2018, which explains why the agency is looking for higher value uses. The Route 49 pilot went a step further by treating the shingle asphalt as part of the binder, which is why the mixes needed a softer base binder and a rejuvenator.That same report demonstrates how slowly the idea moved. A state contract was developed in 2007 to develop a draft specification that would allow up to 5% clean shingles in asphalt; however, no Caltrans district would execute a project and the contract was revoked in 2009. The four mixes later installed on Route 49 were only drafted by Caltrans in 2020 as part of the pilot specification.Laboratory results on plant-produced samples were mixed. In rutting tests on the mixes checked before construction, the control did worst, the shingle-only mix performed best, and the combined mix landed between them. Fatigue tests were split, with the shingle mixes doing better at higher strain levels and the control doing better at lower ones. Chemical ageing tests also suggested a higher risk of block cracking in the shingle mixes once their binder had aged heavily. Earlier work by the same research centre had even reported poor results when shingle binder failed to blend with fresh binder, which was part of the reason for running a proper field trial.Three years in serviceA laboratory cannot fully copy snow, traffic and several summers of heat, so the real verdict had to come from the road. In December 2024, about 3.1 years after paving, UC Davis researchers closed a lane, walked the sections and recorded every crack. The mix with 3 per cent shingles alone showed the most wear, with low-severity alligator cracking along about 6 per cent of its wheel path, mild pumping of fine material through the cracks and slight rutting, the only section to show any. That runs against its laboratory result, where the shingle-only mix rutted least, and it is a reminder that plant-produced samples cannot capture everything a road goes through. The combined mix of 10 per cent recycled pavement and 3 per cent shingles did far better, with alligator cracking along under 1 per cent of the wheel path, less than half the level in the section using recycled pavement alone. The control mix had the least cracking overall.The researchers noted that the old road below was already damaged and reflected cracking was therefore always expected. They also suggest that pumping in the shingle-only section could speed deterioration by causing material loss from the layers below. Further surveys were planned for 2026, and no results from them have been reported yet. One of the two shingle portions cracked less than a basic recycled mix, and a shingle mix can be produced, placed and approved under California’s performance criteria. The other showed the most distress of the four, and three years is a short time in the life of a highway.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2009, Indiana mixed old roofing shingles into a US Route 6 warm-asphalt trial; the road became a real-world durability test, not just a lab experiment
articles.summary: Discover how Indiana's groundbreaking trial in 2009 mixed recycled roofing shingles with warm asphalt on U.S. Route 6, providing valuable insights into real-world pavement performance and durability.
articles.body: When a roof is redone, the old shingles are often taken to a landfill and dumped. US highway agencies have investigated recycling asphalt shingles in pavement for about 25 years, initially using manufacturing waste and later examining shingles removed from existing roofs. These tear-off shingles are harder to reuse because they come from different rooftops and have weathered for years in sun and rain. Engineers therefore needed field evidence to assess how they would perform in real traffic conditions.Indiana began a field demonstration in 2009 to test how recycled shingles performed in asphalt pavement under real traffic conditions. INDOT’s technical brief says the mixes were planned and produced to meet state criteria. The lab tests seemed promising. But the narrative of the road was mixed over the next three years. Cracking occurred in all the test sections, greatest in the warm mix shingle part and least in a normal recycled asphalt mix. And that gives it a useful result precisely because it wasn't a clean win.The trial itselfContractor Phend & Brown completed the renovation in late summer 2009. Underneath was a layer of ancient concrete pavement with a layer of asphalt on top of it, which would be important later on in the story. Crews milled 1.5 inches (about 4 cm) of asphalt and replaced it with one of three pavement mixes. The first was a normal Indiana mix, 15% recycled asphalt pavement, with no shingles. The second, a normal hot mix, had 3% post-consumer shingles. The third used the same 3% shingles in a warm mix with foaming technology, which allows the binder to coat the stone at lower temperatures than hot mix.The recycled shingles were ground finely enough to pass through a half-inch sieve. The shingles themselves contained 26.8% asphalt by weight; this figure describes the shingles’ composition, not their proportion in the pavement mix. The engineers had two questions: Would warm mix technology be detrimental to a shingle mix? How would a shingle recipe compare to the recycled pavement mix that Indiana previously used? Samples were obtained throughout manufacture and sent to the laboratory for testing, and those results dictated the way everyone read the road thereafter.What the laboratory saidIndiana’s endeavour was just a part of a much wider effort. Iowa State University researchers conducted a national pooled fund study from 2009 to 2013, led by Missouri and including California, Colorado, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Minnesota, Wisconsin and the Federal Highway Administration. Each state took a different tack. Some looked at the grind of the shingles, some looked at how much to use, and Indiana looked at the combination with warm mix.With shingles, the greatest effect was in the binder. Old shingle asphalt is substantially stiffer than fresh paving asphalt and will alter the performance grade of the blend. The low temperature grade improved by one step to minus 16 degrees Celsius when 15% recycled asphalt pavement was added, while the high temperature grade remained at 70 degrees. The two mixes containing 3% recycled asphalt shingles had extracted binder graded PG 76-10, compared with PG 70-16 for the mix containing 15% recycled asphalt pavement. The shingle-containing mixes therefore had a higher high-temperature grade but a warmer low-temperature grade, indicating a potential trade-off in cold-weather performance. Foaming did not affect the grade. A firmer binder is more resistant to rutting in summer heat, but it performs less well in cold conditions.The performance tests were more heartening. The flow number results showed that the shingle mixes would perform better than the recycled pavement mix for rutting resistance. Bending beam fatigue tests showed similar behaviour across the mixes, and a low-temperature cracking test showed no substantial difference in fracture energy across the three. A firmer binder is more resistant to rutting in summer heat, but it performs less well in cold conditions. But laboratory data could not capture heavy-vehicle traffic, so the road surveys were more important.What the road showedEngineers surveyed each portion one, two and three years after construction. By the end, all three parts exhibited transverse, longitudinal and fatigue cracking. In its brief, INDOT blames much of the transverse cracking on movement between the concrete slab and the asphalt overlay above it and says heavy truck traffic may be accelerating damage in the wheel tracks. The recycled pavement section, which did not contain shingles, had the least distress, while the warm-mix shingle section had the most. INDOT emphasised that the level of distress may be related to the state of the pavement under the overlay, which no test mix can correct.The broader national study’s final report was published in September 2013. Its summary of field performance after two years found no rutting, wheel-path fatigue cracking or thermal cracking across the demonstration projects, although transverse reflective cracking from underlying jointed concrete was recorded in several states, including Indiana. Indiana’s project appendix documents surveys through March 2012 and reports progression of transverse cracking, along with low-severity fatigue cracking, across the three test sections. The difference reflects the need to distinguish the national summary’s two-year findings from Indiana’s more detailed, three-year observations.Even with warm mix technology, shingles may be blended into a mix that fulfils a state’s criteria, and INDOT found the results promising enough to share with other agencies creating their own rules. The trial showed that asphalt containing 3% recycled shingles could meet INDOT’s quality-assurance requirements. However, cracking developed across all three sections, and the lack of a pre-construction distress survey meant researchers could not conclusively attribute the damage to the shingles rather than movement in the existing pavement beneath the overlay.You use AI every day. articles.title: Florida approved permanent protection for 1,034 acres of Limestone Creek Ranch, a 70-year cattle operation once owned by a governor; the $6.52 million easement keeps the land working inside the Wildlife Corridor
articles.summary: Florida has approved a $6.52 million conservation easement to protect the 1,034-acre Limestone Creek Ranch, ensuring cattle operations continue while preserving vital wildlife habitats within the Florida Wildlife Corridor.
articles.body: Florida approved a $6.52 million conservation easement last month to protect Limestone Creek Ranch in Hardee County from future development.The 1,034-acre property, which was formerly owned by Governor Doyle E. Carlton, has supported cattle ranching for more than 70 years. The agreement was approved by Governor Ron DeSantis and the Florida Cabinet on September 29, 2026, as part of a wider round of conservation measures across the state.The ranch supports an average of 300 head of cattle and includes grazing pasture, native woodland and wetlands. Limestone Creek runs through the property before draining east into the Peace River.Easement protects ranch and wildlife habitatThe conservation agreement prevents future development while allowing cattle operations to continue. The property contains a mix of uplands and wetlands that form part of a wider network of habitats in the region.Limestone Creek Ranch is also enrolled in the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services’ Best Management Practices programme, which promotes agricultural practices designed to protect natural resources.The approval forms part of a wider round of land conservation measures announced by the state on September 29. DeSantis and the Cabinet approved measures covering more than 10,770 acres across Florida, including over 2,700 acres within the Ocala-to-Osceola Wildlife Corridor, with an investment exceeding $72.6 million.“Florida continues to make historic investments to protect the lands and waters that make our state unique,” DeSantis said. “These acquisitions will strengthen the Florida Wildlife Corridor and preserve working lands.”Florida expands conservation programmeThe Limestone Creek Ranch easement was among more than 4,500 acres of working agricultural land approved for permanent protection through the state’s Rural and Family Lands Protection Program.The programme allows farmers and ranchers to retain ownership and continue production while restricting development through conservation easements.Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson said the scheme helps keep productive farmland in private hands while safeguarding the land needed for future food production.“RFLPP is a proven, cost-effective way to keep productive farmland in private hands and ensure it remains available to grow the food Floridians depend on for generations to come,” Simpson said.Since 2019, Florida has invested more than $1.5 billion in land conservation through its Florida Forever programme, according to the state. The funding has enabled the Florida Department of Environmental Protection to acquire more than 500,000 acres for conservation, 92% of which are within the Florida Wildlife Corridor.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1982, Ronald Reagan addressed federal spending on risky coastal construction; he restricted subsidies; a 3.8-million-acre coastal system emerged
articles.summary: Explore how President Reagan's Coastal Barrier Resources Act of 1982 has shaped coastal development, restricted federal subsidies, and saved taxpayers billions while influencing property values and development patterns.
articles.body: Some of America’s most vulnerable terrain consists of barrier islands, sand spits, and the marshes behind them. Every time a hurricane passes, seawater finds its way over them, storms toss them about, and waves strip them. However, for much of the 20th century, federal policies quietly reduced the cost of building there. The same stretches of shoreline were often repaired at public expense after each storm, and flood insurance, road funds, and disaster assistance reinforced the pattern.That cycle stopped in October 1982 when President Ronald Reagan signed the Coastal Barrier Resources Act, which didn’t prohibit anything. The Fish and Wildlife Service said Congress acknowledged that federal policies have long funded and encouraged development on coastal barriers, so it removed the incentive rather than outlawing construction.What the law does in realityThe John H. Chafee Coastal Barrier Resources System identifies coastal areas where most new federal financial assistance is restricted. Exceptions include certain emergency activities, military operations, energy resource activities, and the maintenance of navigation channels. The law does not prohibit construction funded by private, state, or local sources, so development can continue even when federal subsidies are unavailable.What it has savedA 2019 analysis published in the Journal of Coastal Research estimated that the law reduced federal coastal disaster expenditures by $9.5 billion between 1989 and 2013. It projected additional savings of $11.4 billion to $108.6 billion from 2019 to 2068, depending on modelled development rates and disaster-damage scenarios. The estimates are expressed in 2016 dollars. The more recent analysis estimates the annual savings on NFIP claims at about $930 million. Development within the system is much slower than in comparable areas outside it, and individual parcels are less likely to be protected by seawalls and similar hard structures.A 2007 analysis by the Government Accountability Office revealed that around 84% of the system's land was underdeveloped but noted that building was going on regardless in places, aided by commercial interest, local government backing and affordable private flood insurance. It said several federal agencies had also provided prohibited assistance in some cases. A new study examines what happens at the boundaries of these protected areas.The spillover effectThe study also found evidence of a spillover effect: although building density was lower inside designated areas, development density was higher in some nearby areas. Between 1,000 and 2,000 meters from system boundaries, building density was 20% to 47% higher than in comparison areas. Flood insurance claims per acre were 40% to 64% lower in these bordering areas, and the authors estimated that higher development and property values generated about $911 million a year in additional local property-tax revenue.The estimated effect varied by state. Building activity was lower in 10 of the 13 states analyzed, while the estimates were positive in Alabama, Florida and New York. The authors suggested that differences in state and local policies could help explain these variations. The state-level results show that the overall trend did not apply uniformly across every location.More than four decades later, the core idea of the legislation remains unusual. It never dictated to landowners what they could build. It simply announced that Washington would no longer pay for it. The agency now has 942 units in 24 states and territories along the Atlantic, Gulf, and Great Lakes coasts, as well as in Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands, and Congress still has to approve most changes to the map. Whether this market-style strategy can be used elsewhere, as the authors recommend for inland floodplains and wildfire-prone areas, depends on whether legislators are willing to let people bear their own risk.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2025, UK researchers developed self-healing bitumen with oil-filled plant spores, building on earlier lab tests where aged bitumen cracks healed in about 50 minutes
articles.summary: UK researchers have developed a self-repairing road material using plant spores and recycled oils, potentially saving motorists millions in vehicle repair costs. Laboratory tests show it can repair cracks within an hour, extending road lifespan by up to 30%.
articles.body: Researchers have developed a self-healing road material that repairs small cracks before they develop into potholes. The material is made of porous plant spores filled with recycled oils, which are released under pressure from passing traffic. It works by softening the bitumen, letting it flow into cracks and sealing them without the need for any human intervention.According to the Guardian, the research involved a collaboration of scientists with Swansea University and King's College London, alongside Google Cloud. Laboratory tests showed that it would take only an hour to repair small fractures, while Dr Jose Norambuena-Contreras of Swansea University added that the lifespan of road surfaces could increase by 30% if the technology is used. The research addressed the problem of potholes that affect road maintenance across the UK by damaging vehicles, consequently leading to an increase in repair costs and creating hazards for road users. The material stops cracks before they can fully form and provides a solution to minimise the need for conventional repairs.How plant spores mend cracks in road asphalt The mineral components of the asphalt are tethered together by bitumen, which over the course of time hardens and renders the surface of the road vulnerable to cracking. These fractures are the result of traffic loads that lead to water entering the pavement. They are further aggravated by repeated thawing and freezing, which eventually turn the damage into potholes.To address this, the researchers incorporated porous spores containing recycled oils into the bitumen to slow the damage. The approach builds on earlier research published in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces in 2022, when researchers investigated microcapsules made from Lycopodium clavatum, a plant whose spores can serve as protective containers for rejuvenating oils.The researchers used sunflower oil and tested different techniques for loading it into the spores. An efficiency of 93.02 ± 3.71% through vacuum encapsulation was achieved, making it the most effective of the methods examined. At a temperature of up to 204°C, the resulting microcapsules remained stable, while in a fluorescence-based experiment, it took only 50 minutes to heal the cracks in an aged bitumen sample. However, it would be remiss not to mention that the experiment in 2022 and the later development reported in 2025 cannot be treated as identical tests. The earlier study investigated how the microcapsules were prepared and their performance, whereas the later report described a developing road material and its potential application.Machine learning and the prospect of longer-lasting roadsThe research team also used Machine learning to investigate how organic molecules moved within the bitumen, as well as its response when cracks appeared. The effectiveness of self-healing is contingent on the rejuvenating oil's movement and the bitumen's ability to close the damaged area, so understanding these interactions was paramount. According to The Guardian, the researchers believed the material could be scaled up for British roads within a couple of years, but that was a forecast made in February 2025, and with October 2026 now here, that window runs only into 2027, and no large-scale deployment has been confirmed yet.National Highways has also identified self-repairing road surfaces among the technologies being considered to improve road maintenance. However, if the technology performs as expected, then there are financial implications to be considered. The AA reported that £579 million was spent by UK motorists to repair vehicles damaged by potholes in 2024, compared to £474 million in 2023. There is, however, a caveat: whether laboratory healing can actually be translated into real-world durability under real traffic and weather conditions. articles.title: Victoria sold 2.6 hectares of a heritage former psychiatric hospital site to Channel Nine for A$1 million, about A$38 per sq metre; MPs and neighbours are now demanding answers over The Block deal
articles.summary: The Victorian government’s sale of a historic former psychiatric hospital site in Sunbury to Channel Nine for A$1 million has triggered questions over the
articles.body: The Victorian government’s sale of a historic former psychiatric hospital site in Sunbury to Channel Nine for A$1 million has triggered questions over the valuation, transparency and public interest behind the deal. Reporting by Star Weekly, The Guardian and realestate.com.au has highlighted concerns over the price paid for the 2.6-hectare Jacksons Hill property, which is set to feature in the 2027 season of The Block. The transaction, recorded on the Victorian government’s property sales history website, covers three heritage-listed buildings at the former Sunbury Asylum precinct. At approximately A$38 per square metre, the sale has drawn scrutiny from politicians and community members who want to know whether the state secured the best possible return for publicly owned land. Channel Nine acquired the buildings in September for its renovation reality show, with plans submitted for assessment proposing to turn the historic structures into six residential properties. The project is expected to require extensive restoration, with heritage restrictions and the condition of the existing buildings presenting significant challenges.Questions over the sale processDavid Ettershank, a Western Metropolitan MP, raised the transaction in Victoria’s Parliament on September 22, asking the government to disclose the property’s valuation and explain why it had not been offered through an open, competitive sale process. His concerns reflect broader questions about whether other prospective buyers were given an opportunity to put forward offers.Housing, Building and Precincts Minister Nick Staikos responded on October 2, saying the government had approved an exemption from the usual public sale process. The decision followed years of engagement that, according to the government, had failed to identify a financially viable use for the land.The government’s position is that Channel Nine’s proposal provides an opportunity to restore the deteriorating heritage buildings while encouraging further investment in the wider precinct. The sale was approved by the state government’s land monitor, with the government maintaining that the property changed hands at market value. A spokesperson for the Department of Transport and Planning said independent valuers determined the sale price, which was certified by Valuer General Victoria.Why the price is difficult to compareThe reported figure has attracted attention partly because the property is located in a suburb where residential real estate can command substantially higher prices. However, property specialists and government representatives have cautioned against comparing the transaction directly with ordinary residential land sales.Jacksons Hill is not an undeveloped housing block. The site contains three substantial buildings protected by the Victorian Heritage Register, and any conversion must account for the cost and complexity of conservation work. Those obligations can affect what a buyer is prepared to pay and whether a proposed development is financially viable.Reporting by realestate.com.au has also noted that earlier estimates of the sale price differed from the final figure recorded by the government. The confirmed A$1 million amount has intensified debate over how the valuation was calculated and how the costs associated with the site influenced the final price. The redevelopment plans remain subject to heritage assessment, meaning the proposed residential conversion is not simply a matter of renovating the buildings to ordinary housing standards.A historic site’s futureThe former asylum holds considerable historical significance for Sunbury and the wider state. Its future has therefore become a question not only of property value but also of how public heritage assets should be preserved and reused. Supporters of the redevelopment argue that finding a commercially workable use could help prevent further deterioration and bring investment to the precinct. Critics, however, have questioned whether a private television production was the best available route, particularly without an open sale process that could have tested the market.The government has defended the transaction on the grounds that previous efforts to find a viable use had been unsuccessful and that the proposed project could unlock further development opportunities. The central question now is whether the sale price adequately reflects both the property’s constraints and its potential value. With the government standing by its valuation process and critics continuing to seek greater transparency, the Jacksons Hill deal has become a wider debate over accountability, heritage conservation and the use of public land.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘City terrorised by rogue agency’: Mamdani seeks probe into ICE shooting of Dominican man in NYC
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has called for an investigation into an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent’s shooting of a migrant in the
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has called for an investigation into an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent’s shooting of a migrant in the Bronx and the New York Police Department’s response to the incident, while renewing his demand for the federal agency to end its operations in the city.The Democratic socialist mayor accused ICE of behaving more like a terrorist organisation than a law enforcement agency and said its presence was making New York less safe.“The city is still dealing with having been terrorised by a rogue federal agency,” Mamdani said during an interview with MS Now on Sunday.The controversy follows Thursday’s shooting of Oscar Belgal, a 28-year-old Dominican Republic native, who was shot in the neck while travelling in a moving vehicle with his five-year-old son in the backseat.Belgal, who was injured in a confrontation involving federal immigration agents in the Bronx, has a criminal record that includes a 2023 conviction in a grand larceny robbery case.He was also arrested in August 2025 on allegations of selling fentanyl, cocaine and heroin, according to reports. Authorities have also linked him to suspected gang activity and said he had previously terrorised neighbours with a machete.Mamdani, however, focused on the circumstances of the shooting, saying Belgal was in pain after being shot and that the incident had traumatised his young son.The mayor criticised ICE agents for firing at a moving vehicle in broad daylight, questioning their conduct during the confrontation.“It feels as if you’re looking at a mass shooter as opposed to seeing some purportedly representing a federal agency,” he said.Mamdani argued that firing at a moving vehicle carrying a five-year-old child was unacceptable and contrasted ICE’s actions with the New York Police Department’s approach.“There’s a reason why the NYPD would not be shooting at a moving vehicle,” he said, adding that New Yorkers wanted ICE operations to end across the city.The mayor has repeatedly called for ICE to be abolished and has described the agency as “rotten to its core”. Following the shooting, he said he had contacted President Donald Trump to demand that federal immigration enforcement operations in New York City be halted.Mamdani also held discussions with Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin over the incident. However, he acknowledged that the talks, which lasted about two hours, ended without an agreement.“I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorise our communities,” Mamdani said in an earlier statement.The shooting has intensified the dispute between the mayor and the Trump administration over federal immigration enforcement in New York City. articles.title: Jason Mraz bought an old San Diego avocado grove as a retreat in 2004; two decades later it is a 17-acre regenerative farm growing organic avocados, coffee and other crops, with much of its fruit sold locally
articles.summary: When Jason Mraz bought a San Diego-area avocado grove in 2004, he was looking for a place to slow down and reconnect with nature.
articles.body: When Jason Mraz bought a San Diego-area avocado grove in 2004, he was looking for a place to slow down and reconnect with nature. Two decades later, that retreat has grown into Mraz Family Farms, a 17-acre operation cultivating organic avocados, California-grown coffee and other specialty crops. The farm’s own account traces the transformation from an old grove of avocado trees, planted in the early 1970s, to a family-run business focused on healthy soil and regenerative agriculture. Its fruit is sold seasonally, both online and through local shops, restaurants and vendors. The evolution has been gradual, shaped by pruning, replanting and experimentation. Instead of treating the land as a backdrop to his music career, Mraz and his family have made caring for it an ongoing part of their lives.A retreat that became a farmMraz Family Farms describes the property as a former old-growth avocado grove, with tall trees planted in the early 1970s. When Mraz purchased the land in 2004, the farm was not yet a commercial operation. It was a place to live, spend time outdoors and care for the existing trees.The change gathered pace more than a decade later. The family farm says it began converting the property into a new operation in 2015, after deciding that the old trees needed a major reset. The work included “stumping,” a process in which trees are aggressively pruned so they can send out new growth. Some of the original trees were nearing the end of their productive life, so the family began making room for new trees and different crops.That transition required patience. Avocado trees do not deliver an instant return after planting, and the farm’s history describes agriculture as a long game. The family also began exploring coffee, herbs, flowers and bananas, with some crops taking years to become ready for harvest.Growing more than avocadosAvocados remain central to the farm. Mraz Family Farms says it cultivates organic California avocados, including Hass and Reed varieties, alongside California-grown specialty coffee. The farm also lists passionfruit among the seasonal produce available to customers.The variety reflects a broader ambition to make the land more productive and resilient. Rather than rely on a single crop, the farm has developed a layered growing system with trees and other plants sharing the space. Its website describes the operation as a small family business growing exotic and specialty crops, supported by extended family and a farm team.The farm’s avocados have also reached local restaurant customers. In 2014, the San Diego Union-Tribune reported that Mraz’s grove supplied around 34,000 pounds of Hass avocados to Chipotle for use in restaurants near his Oceanside home. That connection brought an unusual celebrity angle to a farm story, but the fruit still travelled from trees to local kitchens as a perishable crop with a seasonal harvest.Today, the farm says it sells fruit seasonally through its website and supplies some local Oceanside grocery stores, restaurants and vendors. Availability depends on the crop and the time of year, rather than a year-round harvest.What regenerative farming means hereMraz Family Farms says it received USDA and California organic certification in 2017 and began practising regenerative agriculture. The farm describes regeneration as a focus on building healthy soil, which it sees as the basis for sustainable growing, clean water and restored habitat.That approach is visible in the way the farm handles plant material. When old trees are pruned or removed, some of the wood is mulched and returned to the soil as compost. The farm says it also leaves tree prunings in forested areas to break down naturally, allowing leaves and branches to return nutrients to the ground.Cover crops are another part of the system. The farm describes planting or maintaining vegetation over the soil so that plants can capture sunlight and carbon while supporting the organisms living underground. In this model, the soil is not treated as empty ground between crops. It is a living part of the farm that needs ongoing care.Regenerative farming is not a single technique or an overnight fix. The farm’s account presents it as a series of practices aimed at improving soil and making the land more productive over time. Its experiments with diverse crops, compost and ground cover are part of that longer effort.Fruit with a local connectionThe farm’s website explains that its produce is sold seasonally, with avocados available in different parts of the year depending on variety. The Hass crop typically has a long “hang time,” meaning the fruit can remain on the tree until it is ready to be picked. Mraz Family Farms says it harvests avocados when orders are placed, then ships them so they can ripen naturally.Local sales provide another route from the grove to consumers. According to the farm’s frequently asked questions, some fruit is supplied to Oceanside shops, restaurants and vendors, though the business does not operate a storefront or regularly sell at farmers’ markets. This keeps the connection to local customers while reflecting the scale of a small farm.The emphasis on seasonality is part of the farm’s identity. Customers cannot necessarily expect every crop to be available at all times, but they can follow the growing cycle as harvests arrive. Coffee, too, requires a different pace from avocados, with growing, processing and roasting adding stages before the beans are ready to drink.The work behind the musicMraz is best known as a singer-songwriter, but the farm has become a substantial part of his life away from the stage. The family farm describes him and his wife, Christina, as owner-operators, working with an extended family and farm team to care for the land and its crops.The transition from retreat to working farm did not happen all at once. It grew from looking after the trees already on the property, recognising that they needed renewal and deciding to make room for a wider range of crops. The result is a business that combines family life, agriculture and local food sales.Two decades after the purchase, the old avocado grove has become a 17-acre experiment in growing food while caring for the soil beneath it. Avocados remain its best-known crop, but coffee, passionfruit and other plantings point to a farm still evolving. For Mraz, the land that once offered a quiet escape has become a long-term commitment, one harvest and one season at a time.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
