articles.title: The Florida mansion featured in Scarface is listed for $237 million; its 2.38-acre waterfront estate was once part of Richard Nixon’s Winter White House retreat
articles.summary: A waterfront property in Key Biscayne, Florida, has two rather different claims to fame.
articles.body: A waterfront property in Key Biscayne, Florida, has two rather different claims to fame. It appeared in the 1983 crime film Scarface as the home of drug dealer Frank Lopez, a character played by Robert Loggia, and the wider estate was once associated with President Richard Nixon’s winter retreat. Fox News reported the residence is being offered for $237 million, placing it among the most expensive properties on the market. Set on 2.38 acres at 485 W. Matheson Drive, the mansion combines a cinematic past with extensive Biscayne Bay frontage, a private marina and a helipad linked to its presidential history. Inside, the house retains a glass elevator familiar to viewers of the film.Inside the Scarface mansion listed for $237 million in Key Biscayne, FloridaThe property became part of Hollywood history through Scarface, the crime drama directed by Brian De Palma and released in 1983. Al Pacino played Tony Montana, a Cuban immigrant who rises through Miami’s criminal underworld, while Michelle Pfeiffer appeared as Elvira Hancock. The mansion, however, portrayed the residence of Frank Lopez, a drug dealer whose position in Montana’s world changes as the story unfolds.Located at 485 W. Matheson Drive, the house was built in the early 1980s. Its connection to the film remains visible in the interior, particularly the glass elevator that featured in scenes from the production. The residence has since become associated with one of the best-known locations from the film, giving the property an identity that extends beyond its architecture and waterfront setting.The $237 million asking price reflects the scale of the estate and its location, alongside its unusual history. The property occupies 2.38 acres in Key Biscayne, an island community south of central Miami, with views across Biscayne Bay towards the city skyline.A waterfront home with room for extensive entertainingReportedly, the mansion measures approximately 13,000 square feet and contains five bedrooms, with a gym that can be converted into a sixth. There are more than seven bathrooms, while large windows bring views of the bay into the main living areas. The open-plan interior includes the glass elevator that links the house's levels and remains one of its most recognisable features.Outside, the estate has 862 feet of direct Biscayne Bay frontage. Its private marina provides space for large yachts, adding a substantial boating facility to the property. The combination of open water, skyline views and dedicated mooring space gives the grounds a different character from a conventional urban mansion.The pool area provides another space for outdoor entertaining, while the property's size allows the house and its waterfront facilities to sit within a sizeable private plot. At this price level, the listing is selling access to the bay as much as the residence itself.How the Key Biscayne estate became linked to Richard Nixon’s Winter White HouseThe mansion's history reaches beyond its role in Scarface. The site was once part of a larger compound used by Richard Nixon as his so-called Winter White House, a name given to locations where the president spent time away from Washington during his administration.Nixon made frequent visits to Florida during his presidency, and the wider Key Biscayne retreat was used for both relaxation and official business. The estate's former presidential helipad is among the features associated with that history. Its presence offers a reminder of the property's earlier role, when the surrounding grounds formed part of a setting used by a sitting US president.The listing identifies the property as having belonged to the larger retreat, rather than suggesting that every part of the present-day residence served as Nixon's personal living quarters. Its history is tied to the broader site and the use of the grounds during his time in office.How the Scarface filming location became part of Hollywood historyFor Scarface fans, the house offers a physical connection to a film that has remained prominent in popular culture for more than four decades. Pacino's portrayal of Tony Montana helped make the production a lasting reference point for crime cinema, with its visual style, dialogue and characters continuing to be recognised well beyond its original release.The mansion's appearance in the film gives prospective buyers an additional point of interest, although its scale and waterfront position are substantial features in their own right. Unlike a property whose screen history survives only through photographs or a commemorative plaque, this residence still contains a recognisable element from its time on camera: the glass elevator.The film was not universally acclaimed when it first appeared, but its reputation grew over time. The Key Biscayne house has become part of that legacy, linking a real estate listing to a particular period in Hollywood filmmaking and to the story of a fictional Miami crime boss.The $237 million listingThe property is being marketed by Jill Eber and Judy Zeder of The Jills Zeder Group at Coldwell Banker Realty. Its asking price is $237 million, attached to a home that combines a substantial waterfront position with a Hollywood association and a connection to American presidential history.The estate's appeal rests on several distinct features. There is the 13,000-square-foot residence, the extensive bay frontage and private marina, as well as the glass elevator that appeared in Scarface. Its association with Nixon's former winter retreat adds another layer to the property's background.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Power cuts disrupt students’ sleep, studies in Madurai village
articles.summary: Madurai’s Pannaikudi village faces 4–6 hour night power cuts, disrupting students’ sleep and studies; residents blocked a road as Tangedco cited line faults.
articles.body: Madurai: For schoolchildren in Pannaikudi near Alanganallur, the struggle to concentrate in classrooms begins the previous night. Power cuts lasting four to six hours disrupt their sleep, leaving them exhausted the next morning and struggling to keep pace with lessons. Frustrated by recurring outages, around 50 students carrying textbooks joined more than 150 residents in blocking the Alanganallur–Mattuthavani Road, bringing traffic to a standstill.“The power cuts usually happen at night. We usually don’t have power from 2am to 6am. This disrupts our sleep, and when power goes off in the evening or there is low voltage, it disturbs our study schedules too,” said Sundar, a student. He said voltage fluctuations also caused headaches, sometimes forcing him to miss school.While prolonged overnight outages have intensified over the past week, residents said they had been facing frequent power disruptions for three months. Repeated complaints to electricity department officials failed to bring relief, prompting the road blockade.For agricultural and daily-wage workers, returning home after a day’s labour has offered little respite. Residents said erratic power supply made household chores difficult, while voltage fluctuations damaged electrical appliances.“The intense heat over the summer in the past few months has intensified the struggle and frustration caused by the power cuts,” said Charan, a farmer from Alanganallur.The problem extends beyond Pannaikudi. On Friday, nearly two dozen villages around Alanganallur and Vadipatti experienced a power outage lasting almost 18 hours. Villagers demanded regular inspections of power lines and quicker restoration of supply when faults occur.Police intervened during the blockade to pacify protesters, who sought a permanent solution rather than temporary restoration.Responding to Saturday’s disruption, Tangedco said a fuse at the Pannaikudi distribution transformer blew at 6pm. Staff replaced it at 6.45pm, but it blew again, prompting an inspection. Officials found that strong winds had caused low-tension power lines to become entangled. articles.title: Kutch man loses ₹94L to online trading fraud
articles.summary: Kutch Adipur man duped of ₹94 lakh in online trading scam via WhatsApp group; fake app showed ₹4.1 crore, then demanded ₹63 lakh fee to withdraw.
articles.body: Rajkot: A 58-year-old Adipur resident was allegedly cheated of more than Rs 94 lakh in an online trading fraud after being lured by promises of double returns. The fraudsters allegedly displayed profits exceeding Rs 3.2 crore in a trading app but demanded a service fee of over Rs 63 lakh when he tried to withdraw his money.Rajesh Maheshwari, who works with a private firm in Gandhidham, lodged a complaint with the cybercrime police station, Kutch East, on Oct 9.According to the complaint, Maheshwari was added to a WhatsApp group on Aug 19, where messages promoted lucrative online trading investments. The group administrator, claiming to represent a trading company called DeltaaialGo, persuaded him to download an app and invest.Maheshwari initially invested Rs 72,920 and received a purported gain of Rs 3,820. Encouraged, he continued investing over the next one-and-a-half months, transferring more than Rs 94 lakh to various bank accounts. The app eventually showed a balance of Rs 4.1 crore, including claimed profits of Rs 3.2 crore.Having borrowed money from friends and taken an Rs 11 lakh loan to fund his investments, Maheshwari tried to withdraw Rs 88 lakh on Oct 5. When the transaction failed, the alleged fraudsters demanded a 20% service fee exceeding Rs 63 lakh before allowing withdrawals. They refused his request to deduct the fee from the displayed balance, prompting him to realise he had been cheated.Police registered a case under Sections 316(2), 318(4) and 3(5) of BNS, along with relevant provisions of the Information Technology Act.Investigating officer B V Borisagar told TOI that police were analysing Maheshwari’s bank statements to trace the recipient accounts and track the movement of funds. Investigators are also trying to identify the app’s creators, the WhatsApp group’s administrators and organisers, and the alleged mastermind. articles.title: To escape ₹40L debt, nephew scripts fake heist
articles.summary: Rajkot man staged fake ₹11 lakh daylight robbery with two friends to dodge ₹40 lakh debt to uncle; trio arrested after CCTV probe and confession.
articles.body: Rajkot: In a bizarre twist, a reported daylight robbery in Rajkot turned out to be an alleged conspiracy by a nephew to evade repayment of debt to his uncle. The accused reportedly staged the theft of a bag supposedly containing Rs 11 lakh, with help of two friends to make the incident appear genuine.Police arrested the main accused Dhirendrasinh Vaghela (32) and his two friends Dhruvrajsinh Gohil and Bhavesh Khuva on Sunday. Police said Vaghela had allegedly promised his accomplices Rs 2.5 lakh for their role in the plan. Gohil had previously been booked in a robbery case, while Khuva also had a criminal history.The three accused are scheduled to be produced before a court on Monday, with police seeking their remand for further investigation.The incident occurred around 2.30pm on the road from Nana Mava Road to Sagar Chowk, under the jurisdiction of Taluka police station on Saturday. Two men on a motorcycle without a number plate allegedly kicked the bike carrying the uncle and nephew from behind before fleeing with the bag.The report prompted senior police officers, including those at the deputy commissioner of police (DCP) level, to rush to the scene. Crime Branch teams examined CCTV footage and tracked the suspects’ movements.However, inconsistencies in the nephew’s account of the incident raised suspicions. During questioning, Vaghela, allegedly failed to explain the source of the money supposedly stolen. He eventually confessed to fabricating the robbery, police said.Investigators found that Vaghela had borrowed around Rs 40 lakh from his uncle, Hardevsinh Zala, about three months ago to fund a vehicle trading business. Zala had reportedly raised the money by pledging gold jewellery. With his uncle pressing him to repay the debt, Vaghela allegedly devised the fake robbery plan about a week before the incident, police said.According to police, Vaghela promised to return Rs 11 lakh and asked his uncle to collect the money. He then accompanied Zala on his motorcycle, carrying an empty red bag. The two accomplices, Dhruvrajsinh Gohil and Bhavesh Khuva, allegedly executed the staged robbery, while Vaghela urged his uncle to chase them to make the incident appear authentic.Crime branch teams traced the suspects towards Kalavad and apprehended Gohil and Khuva on the Kalavad-Jamnagar road. articles.title: 477% excess rain in 24 hrs damages paddy, cotton in Punjab
articles.summary: Punjab saw 477% excess rain in 24 hours, flooding mandis and damaging paddy and cotton; farmers demand immediate crop damage assessment and compensation.
articles.body: Bathinda: Unseasonal rainfall across Punjab has damaged paddy and cotton crops, submerging grain markets and disrupting procurement just as the harvest season gets underway.Punjab recorded 477% excess rainfall in 24 hours from 8:30 am on Saturday, receiving 2.3 mm of rain against the normal of 0.4 mm. Fazilka district topped the list with 28 mm, followed by Faridkot (9 mm), Muktsar (7.7 mm), Pathankot (3.9 mm), Ferozepur (2.4 mm) and Bathinda (1.3 mm).This spike comes after a dry southwest monsoon (June–Sept), during which the state faced a 40% rainfall deficit. As of Oct 10, only 12% of the paddy crop had been harvested.Punjab State Disaster Management Authority (SDMA) has cautioned against thunderstorms, lightning, gusty winds (50-60 kmph), hailstorms and moderate to heavy rains in the next 24 hours in Barnala, Fatehgarh Sahib, Gurdaspur, Jalandhar, Kapurthala, Ludhiana, Malerkotla, Pathankot, Patiala, Sangrur and SBS Nagar districts.In Fazilka, a three-hour storm Sunday morning left the main grain market submerged under nearly three feet of water, leaving heaps of paddy floating. Goldy Sachdeva, president, Fazilka Arhtiya Association, estimated losses at nearly Rs 15 crore and accused officials of ignoring requests to allow crop stacking in private covered yards.Protesting against the inadequate arrangements, the association blocked the Fazilka-Ferozepur national highway on Sunday. Farmers accused the administration of failing to make necessary arrangements at the mandis, saying the lack of drainage facilities caused losses running into lakhs of rupees. Farmers said they had earlier been allowed to keep their paddy in the private yards of commission agents, but the administration had this time prevented them from using the facilities. Sachdeva said piles of paddy had accumulated in the markets due to delays in lifting the crop and a shortage of storage space.Similar flooding was reported in Malout (Muktsar), Mansa, Barnala and Bathinda. Farmer Balkar Singh from Rattakhera village said they have been waiting for their crop to be purchased for the last eight days. “We were told that it would be done Sunday but heavy rain dashed our hopes. Now, the moisture content has risen considerably and we will have to wait longer to sell the crop.“Punjab agriculture department director Gurjit Singh Brar told TOI they are seeking details of damage to crops. He said 88% of the crop is still to be harvested, warning that more rainfall could threaten cotton crop quality if water stagnates in the fields.Punjab State Agricultural Marketing Board chairman Harchand Singh Barsat said proper arrangements have been made for paddy procurement in anticipation of a bumper crop.
